column1: # title: ENG-205 Middle Ages Intro — 2 Names

column2: Honorius was the Roman emperor who recalled the troops from Britain, which left the Britons defenseless.
The Angles, Saxons and Jutes were Germanic tribes who came to Britain as mercenaries after the Romans left and then took over the island, beginning the Anglo-Saxon period.

column1: Where the Angles, Saxons and Jutes settled
column2: The Jutes settled Kent, the Saxons settled Essex, Wessex and Sussex, and the Angles settled East Anglia, Mercia and Northumbria.

column1: Why the Angles, Saxons and Jutes matter to English
column2: The Germanic speech of the Angles, Saxons and Jutes became Old English, and the Angles and Saxons gave the Anglo-Saxon period its name.
Alfred the Great was the first true English king, who united the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms against the Danes.
Alfred the Great organized the kingdom's defense and government by creating the fyrd, a fleet, written law, the Witan, and the shires.
Alfred the Great commissioned the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and supported Latin learning and Bede's Ecclesiastical History.
Bede was a monk whose Ecclesiastical History of the English People is the main source for the period and preserves Caedmon's Hymn.
Caedmon was an illiterate cowherd who became a poet and composed Caedmon's Hymn, the earliest poem recorded in English.
The Vikings, or Danes, were raiders who attacked England and then settled permanently in the eastern region called the Danelaw.

column1: Why the Vikings matter to English unity
column2: As a common enemy, the Vikings pushed the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms to unite under Alfred the Great.

column1: The Vikings' mark on the English language
column2: The Vikings gave English about 2,000 words, including everyday verbs such as "give," "take," and "die."
Edward the Confessor was the Anglo-Saxon king who built Westminster Abbey, and his childless death set off the fight over the English crown.
Harold Godwinson, Earl of Wessex, was chosen king by the Witan after Edward the Confessor died but lost the crown to William at the Battle of Hastings.
William the Conqueror was the Duke of Normandy who led the Norman Conquest and became king of England, putting a French-speaking ruling class in power.

column1: How William the Conqueror held England
column2: William secured his rule by giving land to Norman vassals, building 5,000 to 6,000 castles, and making all landholders swear loyalty to him.

column1: William the Conqueror and the Domesday Survey
column2: William ordered the Domesday Survey, a record of all the land, people and property in England, so the crown could tax them.
Geoffrey of Monmouth wrote the Latin History of the Kings of Britain, which is the source of the Arthurian legends.
Marie de France wrote the Lais in Anglo-Norman French, drawing her stories from Breton sources.
The Gawain poet, also called the Pearl poet, is the anonymous author of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, an Alliterative Revival poem that survives in only one manuscript.
Geoffrey Chaucer was the Middle English poet of The Canterbury Tales and Troilus and Criseyde.

column1: Why Chaucer stands for the merchant class
column2: As the son of a wine merchant who wrote in English, Chaucer represents the merchant class that rose after the plague.
William Langland wrote Piers Plowman, an alliterative dream vision that criticizes post-plague society and the Church and describes the July "hungry gap."
John Wycliffe was a reformer who attacked corruption in the Church and inspired his followers, the Lollards, to begin the first complete English Bible.
The Lollards were followers of John Wycliffe who attacked Church corruption and produced the first complete English Bible.
The Lollards challenged Church authority by putting scripture into English, and they were persecuted and burned as heretics for it.
Julian of Norwich wrote the Book of Showings, a key text in the fourteenth-century trend of Christian visionary writing.
Margery Kempe wrote The Book of Margery Kempe, an account of her own life and religious experiences.
Sir Thomas Malory wrote Le Morte Darthur in prison, producing the great prose collection of Arthurian romance.
William Caxton set up England's first printing press, whose moveable type made fast, identical copies of books possible.
Henry VII won the Battle of Bosworth Field and married Elizabeth of York, which ended the Wars of the Roses.

column1: Henry VII and the end of the Middle Ages
column2: Henry VII founded the Tudor dynasty, and its beginning marks the end of the Middle Ages.
Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries, which ended their role as England's main producers of books.
